justice: The street cross-section allocates most visible space to motor traffic lanes and a wide construction area, while dedicated pedestrian and cycling space is not clearly marked.
Orange temporary barriers on the right protect the work zone but also show that public space is being unequally occupied by road construction rather than balanced for all users.
A broad paved frontage exists along the shop buildings on the left, yet there are no clearly visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or signed crossings to ensure equal access for all social groups.
The long uninterrupted roadway favors through-movement by vehicles more than universal access for walkers or cyclists.
safety: Temporary plastic barriers separate the active carriageway from the unpaved construction zone, which provides some protection from direct vehicle-worksite conflict.
The right side includes a rough dirt surface and roadside work area, creating edge hazards and reducing recovery space if a driver or cyclist drifts outward.
No visible marked crosswalk, traffic signal, or speed-calming device appears along this long straight segment, which may encourage higher vehicle speeds.
Streetlights are present, but the very wide road geometry and sparse visible human activity can still reduce perceived safety for non-motorized users.
livability: A row of low-rise commercial buildings on the left suggests some local service presence and potential daily-use activity.
However, the corridor feels dominated by vehicular movement and road works, with very limited visible public seating, gathering spaces, or pedestrian amenities.
Large trees on the right contribute greenery and environmental quality, improving the overall neighborhood setting.
The long empty roadway and lack of visible people reduce street vitality and everyday social interaction.
sustainability: Dense roadside trees on the right provide substantial green coverage, shade potential, and some ecological benefit.
The absence of clearly visible bike lanes or public transport stops limits support for low-carbon travel choices.
The broad paved road surface and construction zone indicate a highly car-oriented layout with significant impervious area.
Mixed-use frontage with shops can support shorter local trips, which is a modest sustainability advantage.
aesthetics: The continuous row of similarly scaled buildings on the left creates a coherent streetscape edge.
Large mature trees on the right add visual softness, greenery, and contrast to the otherwise wide hardscape.
At the same time, the temporary barriers, dirt work zone, and exposed construction surface reduce visual quality.
The street appears relatively clean and orderly despite the ongoing works, which supports a moderate aesthetic score.
comfort: Tree canopy on the right offers some shade, but the main roadway and left-side frontage appear highly sun-exposed, reducing thermal comfort in hot conditions.
The pavement on the active lane looks relatively smooth for driving, yet the adjacent construction area is rough and uncomfortable for any potential walking or cycling.
No benches, shelters, or rest areas are visible along the corridor, limiting physical comfort for people spending time outside vehicles.
Low visible crowding provides some psychological comfort, but the oversized road width and construction setting can feel inhospitable for non-motorized users.
walkability: A continuous, clearly protected sidewalk is not evident on either side of the road, especially beside the construction area on the right.
No marked pedestrian crossing or pedestrian-priority feature is visible across this very wide roadway, weakening route connectivity on foot.
The long straight carriageway and large setback from destinations make the environment feel car-oriented rather than pedestrian-scaled.
Shopfronts on the left provide some destination value, but the lack of visible walking infrastructure sharply reduces practical walkability.
bikeability: There is no clearly marked or protected bicycle lane visible along this corridor.
The right edge is occupied by a rough construction zone and temporary barriers, leaving little comfortable space for cycling.
The wide straight roadway may allow riding in traffic, but likely higher vehicle speeds increase stress and conflict risk for cyclists.
No bicycle parking, bike symbols, or intersection treatments for cyclists are visible.
